newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac calls early French poll to prepare for euro.
newsitem.headline: Chirac calls early French poll to prepare for euro.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, saying France needed to join a single European currency from a position of strength, dissolved the National Assembly on Monday and called an early parliamentary election for May 25 and June 1.

In a 10-minute televised address, Chirac said he had decided to bring forward the poll by more than nine months so that the French people could "express themselves clearly on the scale and speed of change over the next five years".
Justifying the early vote -- a reversal of his past views -- he assigned a key role to forthcoming decisions on closer European integration, which he said would bring extra prosperity and security.

"To approach these deadlines from a position of strength, to build a Europe that respects the genius of its member nations and is capable of rivalling the great world blocs, your agreement and support are essential," Chirac said.

He also called for a far-reaching reform of the state to make possible cuts in public spending, which were the only way to reduce taxes and welfare charges which weighed too heavily on citizens and discouraged initiative.

The president urged the French to choose "the right path," warning against both the hatred and intolerance of the extreme right and what he called the left's "archaic solutions based on ever more state, ever more spending, ever more tax".

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin accused Chirac of planning a lurch towards "harsher Anglo-Saxon capitalism" and said he had called a rushed poll with a very short campaign to mask the failure of his own policies.
He charged the centre-right government planned a new dose of austerity and was desperate to go to the polls before corruption scandals under investigation engulfed its leading members.
Chirac said a single EU currency was "essential if we want to assert ourselves as a great economic and political power", with the euro on an equal footing with the dollar and the yen.
He said a new mandate would also help France in "difficult negotiations" to secure a fairer sharing of power between Europe and the United States in the NATO defence alliance.

Shortly after the broadcast, Chirac conferred by telephone with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, symbolising close consultation between the two driving forces behind European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Both conservative leaders have declared their intention to clear the domestic political decks to ensure that the euro goes ahead on time in January 1999.
Earlier this month, Kohl brought forward an announcement that he planned to seek re-election in 1998 for the same reason.
Political analysts said Chirac's decision was a bid to secure a safe, though probably sharply reduced, majority before taking fresh austerity measures to qualify France for EMU.
They said the president wanted to get the election out of the way now rather than have to campaign next year at a time of unpopular measures to qualify for the single currency.
The prospect of up to six weeks of political uncertainty with an outside chance of a left-wing victory gave the French financial markets the jitters.
The franc, stocks and bonds all fell. The CAC-40 bourse index ended the day down 0.98 percent after losing 2.59 percent last Friday as election speculation mounted.
The franc hit a one-month low of 3.3772 to the mark but was far from the panic level of 3.58 to the German currency reached on the day of Chirac's inauguration in May 1995.

A SOFRES institute opinion poll published by the daily Le Figaro suggested the ruling centre-right coalition, which holds 464 of the Assembly's 577 seats, would lose about 150 seats but keep a comfortable overall majority.
Communist party leader Robert Hue, who has demanded a referendum on a single currency, said Jospin's shift to a more critical stance on EMU was "undoubtedly a positive evolution".
The president's own mandate will not be directly affected by the vote. Chirac has five more years to serve. But a left-wing victory could make him a premature lame duck.
